messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Policy Analyst
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame was sixty-eight years old when he finally walked into a therapist’s office, a policy analyst whose careful, data-driven mind had always been his greatest asset. Now it felt like a trap. The traumatic event that had upended his life was not a single moment of violence but a creeping, invisible enemy: a life-threatening illness that had nearly killed him two years earlier. He had been hospitalized with a severe bacterial infection that spiraled into sepsis, his organs beginning to fail while doctors fought to stabilize him. He remembered the fluorescent lights of the ICU, the beeping monitors, the prick of needles, and the terrifying sensation of his own body turning against him. That was the moment his relationship with his own flesh had fractured. He survived, but something inside him had not.

In the months that followed, Kwame returned to his job at a state agency, surrounded by policy briefs and spreadsheets. But the concentration that had once made him a reliable analyst had evaporated. He would stare at a page of text, the words blurring, unable to hold a single policy argument in his head before his mind veered back to the hospital room. His body felt constantly tense, as if coiled for a threat he could not see. Even inside his own home—the quiet condo he had shared with his late wife before she passed away a year after his illness—he could not relax. He found himself scanning the rooms, checking his own pulse, listening for any change in his breathing. His body, which had once carried him through decades of work and marriage, now felt like a foreign agent, unreliable, a source of danger.

The memory of his illness did not behave the way he expected. Sometimes, when he tried to recall the hospitalization, he felt absolutely nothing—a flat, numb detachment, as if he were watching a stranger die. He would describe it to himself as “not my own story.” And yet, at unpredictable moments, the memory would slam into him with full sensory force: he would be sitting at his desk, or opening the refrigerator, and suddenly he was back in that bed, the sterile smell in his nostrils, the weight of the oxygen mask. In those moments, the past became the present. He would be so overwhelmed by fear and helplessness that he had to stop whatever he was doing, gripping the edge of the table, waiting for the wave to pass.

Kwame had come to believe that he would never feel normal emotions again. The joy he used to take in his work, the warmth of remembering his wife’s laughter—all of it felt sealed behind a wall. His body kept reacting as if he were still fighting for his life, even when he was perfectly safe. He began to mistrust every sensation: a racing heart meant another crisis, a twinge of pain meant a new infection. He stopped going to the gym because he did not want to feel his heart pound. At home, he avoided looking at his own reflection too long, afraid of what his body might reveal. The hypervigilance was exhausting, and he became isolated. Colleagues noticed his distractibility; he had been passed over for a project lead because he could not complete a report on time.

What finally brought Kwame to seek help was a morning when he woke up already on high alert, his fists clenched, his jaw tight, before he had even opened his eyes. He realized he could not go on like this. His wife’s death had left him without a confidante, and he had no one to tell that he was afraid of his own body, that he felt like a man trapped in a faulty machine. In the therapist’s office, he sat rigidly, his hands resting on his knees, waiting for the moment he would be told he was beyond help. He was afraid of the answer, but he was more afraid of spending the rest of his years as a stranger to himself.
